definition.text: The way buyers and sellers exchanging money for goods, at prices that reflect value and scarcity, tends to share out goods and services well.

facts.text: Prices tell producers what people want, and the less accurate that information, the worse the coordination and the fewer wants are met.
The market mechanism often cannot provide public goods well, because of problems such as the tragedy of the commons; highways needed government planning.
Free market economies leave resources to the private sector, planned economies to the public sector, and mixed economies to both.

definition.text: A firm's ability to raise the price of what it sells above its marginal cost, by controlling supply or demand, without losing all its customers.

facts.text: Firms with no market power, as in perfect competition, are price takers; firms with it are price makers.
How much power firms have depends on market structure: perfect competition and monopoly are the extremes, with monopolistic competition and oligopoly in between.
Power lasts only behind barriers to entry, such as control of scarce resources, economies of scale, better technology or government rules; OPEC's power comes from controlling oil.
It is measured by markups, or more often by concentration ratios and the Herfindahl-Hirschman index, which need only revenue data.
The less elastic the demand a firm faces, the more it can raise price above marginal cost.
Competition law, such as the US Sherman Antitrust Act of 1890, uses measures of market power to judge whether a firm has abused it.
Jean Tirole won the 2014 Nobel Memorial Prize in Economic Sciences for analysing market power and regulation.

definition.text: The combined market share of the largest few firms in a market, such as the top four.

facts.text: The four-firm ratio is 100 per cent for a monopoly and zero for perfect competition.
Studies suggest a ratio between 40 and 70 percent points to an oligopoly.
Concentration measures are the most common gauge of market power because they need only revenue data, though they ignore costs and profits.

definition.text: An analysis of equilibrium in a single market that holds everything else constant except the one change being studied.

facts.text: Alfred Marshall's supply and demand model is the classic partial equilibrium model.
It treats the prices of substitutes and complements and buyers' incomes as given, which makes it much simpler than general equilibrium.
A tariff on French wine raises its price; partial equilibrium ignores the knock-on rise in demand for domestic wine that feeds back and pushes the price higher still.
Such feedback usually changes the size of a price change but not its direction.

title: Price ceiling

definition.text: A limit, set by government or another body, on the highest price that may be charged for a product or service.

facts.text: Governments set price ceilings to protect consumers from goods becoming too expensive.
Economists generally agree that consumer price controls fail at their aims, and many advise against them.
A ceiling set below the market equilibrium price leads to a shortage of supply.
Ceilings can even raise prices by giving competing firms a shared target to collude on; US states with an 18 percent interest cap saw rates just below it.
Ceilings on Helsinki's Hitas apartments cause queuing and mean flats do not go to those who value them most.
Venezuela's food price ceilings from 2003 caused shortages and hoarding.
Some economists, such as Isabella Weber, argue for price caps to fight sellers' inflation, and Paul Krugman became open to them.

contested_note: Most economists say price ceilings backfire, but some, such as Isabella Weber and later Paul Krugman, support price caps against inflation.

definition.text: A price ceiling on housing rents, such as the US rent controls of the 1940s brought in under Franklin D. Roosevelt's Office of Price Administration.

facts.text: As economic models predicted, the US controls cut the supply of rental homes available to returning veterans.
Homeownership and homes for sale rose at the same time, likely because landlords turned rentals into homes for sale.
